analogy.p: A photographer starts with a wide shot (the play), then zooms in to a single detail (a word), and zooms back out to show how the detail fits the landscape (purpose). Examiners want the whole sweep: wide, close, wide. The analogy breaks down because a lens is passive, whereas your analysis must interpret and choose what matters.
analogy.t: The zoom lens on a camera

bullets: Do not memorise one essay; memorise a method so that you can respond to any question.
Each paragraph should touch AO1, AO2 and, where it adds meaning, AO3.
The mark scheme rewards “exploratory” and “conceptualised” responses at the top, so aim for ideas, not description.
Part (a) and part (b) are different tasks: (a) is extract-based and analytical; (b) asks for recalled quotations from elsewhere. See the next note for the part (a) method.

callouts.p: Mark allocations and AO weightings can vary; confirm which AOs are assessed in each part on your own paper and specimen materials.

core.h: Decoding the assessment objectives (AO1 to AO4)
core.p: The mark scheme rewards four things. AO1 is your response and argument, supported by well-chosen quotations. AO2 is analysis of the writer’s language, form and structure with subject terminology. AO3 is understanding of context and how it relates to the text. AO4 is accurate vocabulary, spelling, punctuation and sentence structure; it is assessed on the Shakespeare and post-1914 questions only. Check the marks for each part on your paper, as the distribution can change between parts (a) and (b).

head: AO
What it rewards
What it looks like in a Macbeth answer
rows: A critical, personal, well-structured response with textual references
A clear thesis, a line of argument, short precise quotations from across the play
Analysis of language, form and structure; use of terminology
Zooming in on a single word, commenting on soliloquy, rhythm, structure and effect
Understanding of the relationships between text and context
Divine right, witchcraft, Gunpowder Plot, Great Chain of Being used to explain effects
Accurate spelling, punctuation, vocabulary and sentence structure
Correct spelling of names and key terms; varied and controlled sentences

bullets: “Explore how Shakespeare presents…” asks for methods and effects, not a list of features.
“How far do you agree?” asks for a judgement and an alternative view.
“In this extract” (part (a)) means stay inside the printed extract; “elsewhere in the play” (part (b)) means use recalled moments from other scenes.
“In the play as a whole” means choose moments from across the acts.
Focus words, such as “ambition”, “guilt” or “power”, should recur in your topic sentences.
Underline words like “presents” and “ideas”: they point you to the writer’s methods.

callouts.p: If the question is about “ambition”, say the word in every topic sentence in a slightly different form (ambition, aspiration, hunger, drive).

core.p: Many marks are lost before writing begins because students answer the question they hoped for. Underline the command word (explore, how, to what extent), the focus (a character, a theme, an idea) and the scope (in this extract, elsewhere in the play, in the play as a whole). Then restate the question as a problem to solve: what is the argument I can make about this focus?

head: Question focus
Possible conceptual angle
rows: Power through rejecting femininity, then undone by it
Imagination to emptiness; a hunger that devours
Temptation is not compulsion; choice remains
Sacred trust; regicide as cosmic crime
Masks as survival and as moral decay
Imagination punishing the body; sleep and blood

bullets: Use a stem: “Shakespeare presents… as… so that…” or “Through… Shakespeare suggests…”.
Avoid vague words such as “good”, “bad”, “important”.
Include a tension where you can: “both victim and agent”, “a hero and a tyrant”.
Your thesis should predict your paragraph order.

callouts.p: A one-sentence argument that names an idea or pattern (not just a topic) and can be developed in stages across the whole essay.

core.p: A thesis is a one-sentence answer to the question that makes a claim someone could disagree with. A conceptual thesis goes further: it names an idea (a pattern, a development, a tension) that can organise the whole essay. It usually has the shape: “Shakespeare presents X as Y, in order to show Z”. The thesis tells the examiner that you are writing with a purpose.

head: Level
Example for “presentation of ambition”
Why
rows: Macbeth is ambitious and kills Duncan.
Shakespeare presents ambition as a destructive force which leads Macbeth to murder.
Shakespeare presents ambition as a hunger that begins in imagination, turns to action under pressure and ends in emptiness.
Conceptual, develops across the play, gives a structure

bullets: Paragraph 1: set up the idea (often early in the play or the extract).
Paragraph 2 and 3: develop or complicate it (a turning point, a contrasting character).
Paragraph 4: climax or reversal (often late in the play).
Optional paragraph 5: alternative interpretation or counter-argument.
Conclusion: evaluate Shakespeare’s purpose, not a repeat of the introduction.
Check that your plan includes moments from at least three acts for part (b).

callouts.p: Spend a short, fixed planning slot on each answer. A plan makes the writing faster and the argument tighter. Adjust to your own pace and your paper’s guidance.

core.p: A grade 9 plan is short but exact. Write the thesis at the top, then list four or five paragraph ideas in a sensible order (usually chronological or by development of the idea). Under each, write one short quotation you can recall perfectly, a technique or structural point, and a context link if it adds meaning. Keep the plan to a few lines per paragraph so that you spend your time writing.

head: Plan slot
Fill with
rows: One short phrase you remember exactly
Where in scene or play, and effect of the placement
One link that explains audience response

bullets: Claim: a point that develops the thesis, not a summary of events.
Quote: embed it in your own sentence, so the grammar flows.
Zoom: pick one word and analyse connotations (what it suggests beyond its meaning).
Structure: say where in the play or scene it appears and what that placement does.
Context: only where it changes the meaning for a Jacobean audience.
Purpose: end by saying what Shakespeare wants the audience to feel or think.
Alternative: “could also suggest”, “alternatively”, to show exploratory thinking.

callouts.p: Pick the most powerful single word in your quotation and write two sentences about it. This is where AO2 marks cluster.

core.h: Writing the analytical paragraph: the zoom
core.p: The paragraph is where marks are earned. Start with a claim that links to your thesis, support it with a short quotation, then zoom in on a word or phrase and explain its connotations and effect. Zoom out to structure: where does this occur and why? Add context where it explains the effect, and finish by linking back to Shakespeare’s purpose. Not every paragraph needs every move, but most should have at least four.

head: Move
Sentence starter
rows: Placed at the end of the soliloquy, this…
A Jacobean audience, who believed…, would…

bullets: Choose phrases of two to six words so they are easy to recall and embed.
Pick quotations with strong single words (“vaulting”, “unsex”, “serpent”, “candle”).
Spread them across acts: at least one from each of Acts 1, 3 and 5.
Learn the context and technique that goes with each, not just the words.
If you cannot recall a quotation exactly, paraphrase or describe the image; do not invent.
Use the quote bank below on this page to practise the “zoom” on each phrase.

callouts.p: A wrong quotation costs marks and credibility. If unsure, describe the image (for example “the dagger soliloquy”) and analyse the technique.

core.h: Choosing and memorising quotations for part (b)
core.p: In part (b) you do not have the text in front of you, so you need a bank of short quotations that you know perfectly. The best quotations are short, rich in language and flexible across themes. Aim to memorise eight to ten, each from a different part of the play, and practise using the same quotation for different questions.

head: Theme
Flexible quotations to learn
rows: “vaulting ambition”; “I dare not wait upon I would”
“unsex me here”; “the milk of human kindness”; “I dare do all that may become a man”
“the serpent under’t”; “False face must hide what the false heart doth know”
“Sleep no more”; “Out, damned spot”; “What’s done cannot be undone”
“Fair is foul, and foul is fair”; “this supernatural soliciting”
“the Lord’s anointed temple”; “this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen”
“Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow”; “Out, out, brief candle!”

bullets: Context options for Macbeth: James I and divine right; the Great Chain of Being; the Gunpowder Plot and equivocation; witchcraft belief; gender expectations.
Weave the context after analysing a word: “…which a Jacobean audience would read as…”.
Spell correctly: Macbeth, Banquo, Duncan, Macduff, Fleance, Malcolm, Donalbain, Dunsinane, Birnam, Cawdor, Glamis, Inverness, soliloquy, tyrant, regicide, sacrilege.
Use semi-colons, colons and subordinate clauses deliberately, not showily.
Write in the present tense: “Shakespeare presents…”, “Macbeth says…”.
Reread your last paragraph to check endings and names.

callouts.p: Use “suggests”, “could imply”, “perhaps” to show you are interpreting, not stating facts.
AO4 is assessed on the Shakespeare and post-1914 question, so careful spelling and punctuation matter here more than in the other literature papers.

core.h: AO3 and AO4: context and accuracy
core.p: Context should explain the effect of a moment on the original audience or show how an idea reflects the time. It should be brief, precise and tied to the text. AO4 rewards accurate spelling and punctuation and varied sentence structures, so safe handling of names and key terms matters. A few lost spellings are not fatal, but a pattern of errors in names such as Banquo or Macduff will cost marks.

bullets: Does the introduction give a thesis that answers the question?
Does each paragraph begin with a claim that links to the thesis?
Is every quotation short, accurate and embedded?
Have I analysed at least one single word in each paragraph?
Have I commented on structure (where, why, effect)?
Is context linked to meaning rather than listed?
Have I offered at least one alternative interpretation?
Does my conclusion evaluate Shakespeare’s purpose and avoid repeating the introduction?

callouts.p: Mix short, punchy sentences with longer analytical ones; start some sentences with a subordinate clause (“Although…”, “By ending the scene with…”).

core.p: A short checklist before and after writing keeps you on track. Use it in revision so the habits become automatic. In the exam, a quick check of the thesis against your final paragraph can show whether you have sustained the argument.

plan: Ambition as imagination: the aside and soliloquy (Act 1 Sc 3 and Sc 7)
Ambition as pressure: Lady Macbeth’s manipulation (Act 1 Sc 5 and Sc 7)
Ambition as tyranny: the murders and the loss of conscience (Act 3 and Act 4)
Ambition as emptiness: the final speeches (Act 5)
Conclusion: Shakespeare’s warning about unchecked desire
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents ambition in Macbeth.
essays.text:
Shakespeare presents ambition as a hunger that begins in the imagination and ends in emptiness. Rather than treating it as a heroic drive, he shows it corroding the moral order and consuming the man who feeds it.

The play suggests that ambition first lives in the mind. After the witches’ prophecy, Macbeth’s aside shows him wrestling with “this supernatural soliciting”, a phrase in which the abstract noun “soliciting” admits that he is being tempted rather than commanded. The balanced clause that follows, which says it can be neither good nor ill, shows a mind trying to reason and failing. Shakespeare allows the audience to hear this internal debate in a soliloquy or aside, so that his later actions seem chosen. By Act 1 Scene 7 Macbeth names his only motive: “vaulting ambition”. The equestrian image of a rider who leaps too far predicts his fall, and the sentence breaks off at its climax, mirroring a mind that cannot complete the thought. For a Jacobean audience, who believed that killing an anointed king would damn the killer, this admission shows that Macbeth understands exactly what he risks.

Ambition is turned into action by pressure. Lady Macbeth’s fear that her husband is “too full o’ the milk of human kindness” defines kindness as weakness, and her call on the spirits to “unsex me” shows ambition demanding that she reject her nature. Her taunt that Macbeth would live a coward in his own esteem, letting “I dare not” wait upon “I would”, uses antithesis to compress his dilemma. Macbeth’s reply, “I dare do all that may become a man”, shows he has a moral code; her reply redefines manhood as violence. Structurally, the scene ends with Macbeth’s rhyming couplet “False face must hide what the false heart doth know”, a neat closure that sounds like a decision sealed.

Once he is king, ambition becomes tyranny. “Things bad begun make strong themselves by ill” shows Macbeth bound to further crime, and the heavy monosyllables sound like a trap closing. By Act 4 he vows that the very firstlings of his heart shall be the firstlings of his hand, which shows conscience replaced by impulse. A reader might argue that this is still the same ambition, now defended by violence; another might say that the ambition has transformed into paranoia, since he now fears Banquo’s line more than he desires anything.

The final act shows the cost. When Macbeth hears of his wife’s death he speaks of “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow”, a triple repetition which makes time drag, and he calls life a “brief candle”. The imagery of light, once linked to Duncan’s virtue, is reduced to a candle to be snuffed out. The man who wanted everything now finds meaning in nothing, which is the final irony of ambition.

In conclusion, Shakespeare uses ambition as a lens on power, gender and conscience. Macbeth’s fall confirms the Jacobean view that to unseat a sacred order is to unseat oneself.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents ambition not as a driving virtue but as a hunger that corrodes the moral order and consumes its owner: it begins as imagination, becomes action under pressure and ends as empty repetition.
why: AO1: opens with a conceptual thesis (imagination, pressure, tyranny, emptiness) that gives each paragraph a purpose.
AO2: zooms in on specific words (“soliciting”, “vaulting”, “unsexed”) and comments on structure (breaking off, couplet closure, repetition).
AO3: context woven in (divine right, Jacobean view of damnation) as explanation of effect.
Alternative interpretations in the tyranny paragraph (continuation versus transformation).
AO4: precise terminology and controlled sentence variety; names and quotations spelled accurately.

model: Thesis: guilt is physical and imaginative, moving from hallucination to breakdown
Paragraph 1: “Sleep no more” (Act 2 Sc 2): imagined voice, loss of rest
Paragraph 2: ghost scene (Act 3 Sc 4): guilt made public
Paragraph 3: “Out, damned spot” (Act 5 Sc 1): prose, repetition, breakdown
Paragraph 4: contrast with “A little water” and Macbeth’s numbness in Act 5
Context/alternative: Jacobean damnation; or guilt as psychological rather than supernatural
exam.q: Write a conceptual thesis and a four-paragraph plan (with one short quotation each) for: Explore how Shakespeare presents guilt in Macbeth. (8 marks)
exam.tip: Planning marks (invented value) reward clarity and range. Include at least three acts.

model: Identify weaknesses: description, no development, no concept
Add a concept: power through rejecting femininity
Add a development: she controls Act 1, loses control by Act 3
Example: ‘Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a figure who gains power by rejecting her femininity, only to be destroyed by the guilt she denies.’
exam.q: Improve this thesis: “Lady Macbeth is a strong woman who helps Macbeth kill Duncan.” Rewrite it as a grade 9 thesis. (4 marks)
exam.tip: A good thesis names an idea and a shape.

model: “vaulting ambition”: equestrian metaphor; zoom on “vaulting”
“unsex me here”: imperative; zoom on “unsex”
“I dare do all that may become a man”: antithesis; zoom on “dare”
Show how each can serve two questions
Link each to a context if appropriate
Explain the effect on the audience
exam.q: Choose three quotations that you could use to answer both a question on ambition and a question on gender. For each, name a technique and a word to zoom in on. (6 marks)
exam.tip: Flexible quotations are the key to part (b).

model: Add a claim linked to a thesis
Embed “vaulting ambition” in a sentence
Zoom on “vaulting” (energy, risk, rider image that overshoots)
Structural comment: end of the soliloquy; broken sentence
Context: divine right and damnation of regicide
Purpose: warning about unchecked desire
exam.q: Rewrite this weak paragraph to add AO2 and AO3: ‘Macbeth is ambitious. He says vaulting ambition. This shows he is ambitious. In Jacobean times people believed in kings.’ (6 marks)

model: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” as paradox and chiasmus
Pathetic fallacy of thunder, lightning and chant rhythm
Structural choice: witches before any human character
Link to “So foul and fair a day I have not seen”
Link to Lady Macbeth’s “serpent under’t”
Context: Jacobean fear of hidden evil
exam.q: Explore how Shakespeare uses the opening of the play to introduce the idea of appearance and reality. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Mark value is a best guess; check your paper. Use the plan: thesis, four ideas, structure and context.

model: Agree: “vaulting ambition” as the only spur
Disagree: Lady Macbeth’s pressure and the witches’ temptation
Disagree: his conscience and imagination as destabilising
Structure: how ambition escalates to tyranny
Context: Jacobean views on sin and providence
Evaluation: ambition as root, other factors as accelerants
exam.q: “Ambition is the only cause of Macbeth’s downfall.” How far do you agree? (20 marks)
exam.tip: A judgement question needs a clear position and a weighed counter-argument.

mistakes.r: Make a short plan with thesis, paragraph ideas and one quotation each; it saves time and improves structure.
Use the plot only as evidence for an argument about ideas and methods.
Name the device only when you can explain its effect on meaning and audience.
Use short phrases and analyse single words inside them.
Place context inside the analysis where it explains an effect.
mistakes.w: Bolting context on at the end.

mistakes.r: Add “could also suggest” with a second, plausible reading.
Evaluate Shakespeare’s purpose and the overall meaning of the play.
mistakes.w: Repeating the introduction in the conclusion.

mistakes.r: Learn the names and key words so AO4 marks are secure.
mistakes.w: Ignoring spelling of names and terms.

quotes.a: Lady Macbeth instructs Macbeth to appear innocent while being deadly. “Serpent” carries the biblical connotation of the devil in Eden, so she is aligning herself with evil even as she uses it practically. This quotation is flexible: use it for appearance and reality, gender, Lady Macbeth’s manipulation, the Gunpowder Plot fear of hidden traitors and the garden of Eden. A multi-purpose quotation is gold for part (b).
quotes.c: Post-1605 fear of traitors; Garden of Eden.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 5, Lady Macbeth to Macbeth

quotes.a: She asks to be stripped of her gender because she equates femininity with weakness. The imperative “unsex” is a coined, forceful verb that shows she wants to rewrite nature. It supports essays on gender, power, the supernatural (she invokes spirits) and ambition. Alternative reading: she is trapped by Jacobean limits on women, so can only access power by rejecting womanhood.

She fears that Macbeth is too gentle to seize the crown. “Milk” associates kindness with nurture and femininity, which she distrusts. The phrase contributes to arguments about manliness, conscience and character. It also shows how Shakespeare lets Lady Macbeth judge her husband accurately: he does have a conscience.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 5, Lady Macbeth on Macbeth’s nature

quotes.a: She mocks him as a cat in a proverb, letting fear wait on desire. The balanced structure of “I dare not” and “I would” compresses his dilemma into a single phrase. It supports essays on ambition, courage, manhood and Lady Macbeth’s persuasion. Its rhythm makes it easy to remember.
quotes.q: I dare not wait upon I would
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 7, Lady Macbeth taunting Macbeth

quotes.a: Macbeth defines manhood as honour with limits: a man who dares more is not a man at all. This shows he still has a moral code, which Lady Macbeth then overrules. It is perfect for arguments on conscience, manliness and the tragic flaw, and shows Shakespeare setting up the choice.
quotes.q: I dare do all that may become a man

quotes.a: In a startling simile, pity becomes a helpless baby riding the wind, so cruelty will provoke universal tears. The vulnerable infant contrasts with the later murder of children and Macbeth’s own childlessness. It suits essays on conscience, children, innocence and imagery. Alternative reading: the image foretells that innocence will be crushed.
quotes.c: Christian ideals of innocence and mercy.
quotes.q: Pity, like a naked new-born babe

quotes.a: The rhyming couplet at the end of the scene settles Macbeth’s resolve: he will wear a mask. The repetition of “false” stresses hypocrisy, and the neat couplet sounds like a decision sealed. It fits appearance versus reality, kingship, treachery and the Gunpowder Plot fear of dissemblers. As an ending, it makes a structural point about how scenes close on a tidy rhyme.
quotes.q: False face must hide what the false heart doth know

quotes.a: In her last scene she acknowledges that the crime cannot be reversed. The phrase answers her earlier confidence that “what’s done is done” (Act 3). The shift shows how guilt has overturned her certainty. It suits essays on guilt, Lady Macbeth’s arc, structure and irony, and gives a ready example of echo.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 1, Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, closing lines

quotes.a: Life is likened to a candle that burns briefly and is snuffed out. The exclamation and repeated “out” sound like an extinguishing breath, and light imagery returns to the play’s themes of darkness. This is perfect for essays on tragedy, mortality, light and dark, and Macbeth’s final state of mind.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 5, Macbeth’s speech after learning of Lady Macbeth’s death

quotes.a: Macbeth considers the witches’ words and says they can be neither wholly good nor wholly bad. “Soliciting” means tempting or urging, and he admits to being tempted. This suits essays on the supernatural, fate and free will, ambition and conscience. The line shows that he reasons through it, so it supports a responsibility argument.

summary: Learn a repeatable grade 9 method for any Macbeth essay: decode the question and assessment objectives, build a conceptual thesis, plan four or five analytical paragraphs with short quotations, zoom from word to purpose, weave in context and keep spelling and punctuation secure.

terms.d: A one-sentence argument that answers the question and can be developed across the essay.
The ideas or feelings that a word suggests beyond its literal meaning.
A short quotation woven into your own sentence so that the grammar flows.
A group of words linked by the same subject, such as blood or darkness.
A decision about order, pace, placement or shape, such as the opening scene or the ending of a soliloquy.
Words such as “suggests” or “could imply” that signal interpretation rather than fact.
An alternative view that you acknowledge and weigh.
Subject-specific words used accurately, such as metaphor, juxtaposition or soliloquy.
